subject: Model syntax for basic SEM with quadratic term

messages.author: a3c08224aeda8f91
messages.subject: Model syntax for basic SEM with quadratic term
parts:
Hello, 

I am sure this might be a very basic question, but I am just using lavaan and SEMs for the first time in my MS thesis. I am trying to set up a basic SEM in which I can test the effects of percent cover and silicate concentrations on recruitment counts and test silicate effects on percent cover. I want to test both the linear and quadratic effects.
Currently, I have the model set up as such: 

sem_model <- '
  # Polynomial terms: recruits and percent_cover (quadratic)
  logsum_total ~ percent_cover + percent_cover_sq
  logsum_total ~ silicate_avg + silicate_avg_sq
  percent_cover ~ silicate_avg + silicate_avg_sq
'

However, in my results, the model fit is not good. Is this likely a result of a smaller sample size and could be "fixed" with bootstrapping or is something with my model syntax limiting the output of the model? 

Thank you!

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Model syntax for basic SEM with quadratic term
parts:
Model fit is about constraints (that do not match the data). The constraints in your model are (given the way lavaan defaults work) the "cover" variables are nopt allowed to directly predict percent_cover like they do "logsum_total". Modification indices should confirm this. You are also not allowing an interaction effect between the silicate and cover variables, but that omission is unlikely to manifest in lack of fit. If you allow the "cover" variables to have direct effects on "percent_cover", your degrees of freedom will go to 0 and the issue of fit will become moot as the model will have trivially perfect fit. If you were investigating whether the exclusions in your model were consistent with the population from which your data were sampled, then you already have your answer.
The lack of fit could also be the result of distributional issues--nonnormal distributions that violate the multinormality assumption underlying the default maximum likelihood estimator. With "percent" variables, this violation seems likely, but whether there is an effect on lack of fit is hard to say from here. Howevere, it could be that a different transformation of your base variables (carrying over into transformed squared variables) might produce a solution with much better (or worse) fit.
